entry.title: When food goes on the floor
entry.summary: Davies treats food throwing as a moment to understand and set a limit. She suggests asking whether the child is finished, rather than assuming every throw means the same thing.
entry.cue: Food is being dropped or thrown, and you are trying to understand what happens next.
detail: In her example, the adult asks whether the child is finished and offers an “all finished” gesture and help carrying the plate to the kitchen. If the child is not finished eating but keeps throwing food, Davies describes helping take the plate to the kitchen, calmly and without a threat.

The wider eating section remains relevant: her aim is shared meals and child participation, with medical or other food-related concerns taken seriously. The example is not a way to decide that a child has eaten enough.

ageContext.bookAge: No fixed age in the toddler food-throwing passage.
ageContext.readiness: Food is being thrown; the adult asks what the child may be communicating.
ageContext.note: Food throwing alone does not establish that a child has eaten enough.

displayContext.footer: You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have.
displayContext.colophon: Original summaries inspired by The Montessori Baby and The Montessori Toddler. Open any idea for its book references. The illustration is an invitation to explore, rather than a room to reproduce. Follow your child’s pace.
